subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 13! In this unit you will become confident with angles – how to name them, measure them, draw them, and calculate unknown angles using clever geometric rules. Angles are all around you. When Amina watches the hands of the masjid clock move towards Dhuhr, when Hassan tilts the roof of a goat shelter so the rain runs off, or when Yusuf lines up a football shot towards the goal, they are all using angles, whether they know it or not.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Describe an angle as an amount of turn, measured in degrees (°).
Classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex, or a full turn.
Estimate the size of an angle using benchmark angles such as 45°, 90° and 180°.
Measure angles accurately with a protractor, choosing the correct scale.
Draw angles of a given size using a protractor and ruler.
Use the fact that angles on a straight line add to 180°.
Use the fact that angles around a point add to 360°.
Use the fact that vertically opposite angles are equal.

concepts.title: What Is an Angle?
concepts.explanation:
An angle is formed when two straight lines meet at a point. That meeting point is called the vertex, and the two lines are called the arms (or sides) of the angle. But an angle is not really about the lines themselves – it is about the amount of turn or opening between them.

Picture Hassan opening the door of a shop. When the door is only slightly ajar, the angle between the door and the wall is small. As he pushes the door wider, that angle grows. If he opens it until the door lies flat against the next wall, it has swung through a very large angle. The door has not changed its length – only the turn has changed. This is the single most important idea in the whole unit: the size of an angle depends only on the amount of turn, not on how long the arms are.

This catches many learners out. If you draw a 40° angle with short arms, and then draw another 40° angle with very long arms, they are the same size angle. The long arms might look bigger, but the opening between them – the turn – is identical. Whenever you judge an angle, look at the spread between the arms, not their length.

We measure angles in degrees, written with a small circle symbol °. A complete turn all the way around a point is 360°. This number comes from the ancient Babylonians, who counted in sixties; they chose 360 for a full circle because 360 can be divided evenly in so many ways (by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 and more), which makes sharing a circle into equal parts very convenient.
concepts.example: A good way to feel angle size is to imagine standing in the centre of a large clock face and turning. If you face 12 and turn to face 3, you have turned a quarter turn, which is 90°. Turn on to face 6 and you have made a half turn, 180°. Carry on to face 9 and you have made a three-quarter turn, 270°. Return to 12 and you have completed a full turn, 360°. Holding these four benchmark turns in your mind – 90°, 180°, 270°, 360° – gives you a mental ruler for every angle you meet.

concepts.title: Types of Angles
concepts.explanation:
Sorting angles into types helps us describe them quickly. Each type covers a range of sizes, and every angle you ever meet belongs to exactly one type. Learn these ranges carefully – they appear again and again.

Acute angle: greater than 0° and less than 90°. The word ‘acute’ means sharp, and these angles look sharp and pointed – like the tip of a pencil or a thin slice of mango.

Right angle: exactly 90°. This is a quarter turn. The corners of books, tables, windows and doorways are right angles. Two lines meeting at a right angle are called perpendicular. A right angle is often marked with a small square in the corner instead of a curved arc.

Obtuse angle: greater than 90° and less than 180°. The word ‘obtuse’ means blunt. A wide-open book or a gently sloping roof shows an obtuse angle.

Straight angle: exactly 180°. This forms a straight line – a half turn. The hour and minute hands of a clock at 6:00 make a straight angle.

Reflex angle: greater than 180° and less than 360°. These are the ‘big’ angles, the larger opening you get when you go the long way round. Turning almost all the way around to look behind you sweeps a reflex angle.

Full turn: exactly 360°. A complete rotation that brings you back to where you started.

Notice how the boundary values 90°, 180° and 360° are the fence-posts between the types. An angle of exactly 90° is a right angle, not acute and not obtuse. An angle of exactly 180° is a straight angle, not obtuse and not reflex. Being careful at these boundaries stops many mistakes.
concepts.example: Khadija finds it helpful to sort angles the moment she sees them. Shown a 35° angle she thinks ‘smaller than a right angle, so acute’. Shown a 155° angle she thinks ‘bigger than a right angle but not yet a straight line, so obtuse’. Practising this quick sorting builds strong angle sense.

concepts.title: Estimating Angles
concepts.explanation:
Before you ever pick up a protractor, you should estimate the angle. An estimate is a sensible judgement of size based on the benchmark angles you already know. Estimating first is a habit that protects you: if your careful measurement is wildly different from your estimate, you know at once that something has gone wrong – usually that you read the wrong scale on the protractor.

The most useful benchmark is the right angle, 90°, because you can picture it easily as a square corner. Half of a right angle is 45°. A third of a right angle is about 30°, and two-thirds is about 60°. Once you can picture 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°, you can estimate almost any acute angle by asking which of these it is closest to.

For larger angles, build on the right angle. An angle a little past square is about 120° (that is 90° + 30°). A wide obtuse angle is about 135° (90° + 45°) or 150° (90° + 60°). A straight line is 180°. To estimate a reflex angle, estimate the smaller angle on the other side and subtract from 360°.

Here are the handy reference angles worth memorising:

30° is about one-third of a right angle.

45° is exactly half of a right angle.

60° is about two-thirds of a right angle.

90° is a right angle – a square corner.

180° is a straight line – two right angles.
concepts.example: Practise estimating angles in your own surroundings. Look at the angle a laptop screen makes when it is open, the slope of a staircase, the spread of an open pair of scissors, or the angle between the hands of a clock at different times. Guess first in degrees, then check if you can. Zahra plays an ‘angle of the day’ game where she estimates one real angle each morning – over a few weeks her guesses became remarkably accurate.

concepts.title: Measuring Angles with a Protractor
concepts.explanation:
A protractor is the tool made specially for measuring and drawing angles. Most protractors are a clear half-circle marked with degrees from 0° to 180° around the curved edge. Look closely and you will find the important parts:

The baseline (or zero line): the straight edge running along the bottom.

The centre point: a small cross or hole in the middle of the baseline. This must sit on the vertex.

The scale: the numbers around the curved edge.

Two scales: an inner scale and an outer scale, one running left-to-right and the other right-to-left, so you can measure angles that open either way.

Follow these four steps every time you measure an angle:

Place the centre point of the protractor exactly on the vertex of the angle.

Turn the protractor so that one arm of the angle lies along the baseline (the 0° line).

Follow the other arm out to the curved edge and read the number where it crosses.

Choose the correct scale: start from the 0° on the arm you lined up, and count round. Your estimate tells you which of the two numbers is right.
concepts.example: The single most common mistake is reading the wrong scale. Because the protractor has two sets of numbers, the other arm may cross near both a small number and a large number – for example 50° and 130°. This is exactly why you estimate first. If the angle clearly looks acute (sharp, less than a square corner) then the answer must be 50°, not 130°. If it looks obtuse then it must be 130°. Idris always whispers his estimate before he reads, so the protractor can never trick him.

concepts.title: Drawing Angles with a Protractor
concepts.explanation:
Drawing an angle is the reverse of measuring one. Suppose you want to draw an angle of 62°. Follow these steps carefully, and your angle will be accurate:

Use a ruler to draw one straight arm. Mark the vertex clearly at one end.

Place the centre point of the protractor on the vertex, with the baseline lying exactly along your drawn arm.

Starting from 0° on the scale that runs along your arm, count round to 62° and make a small, neat dot at that point.

Remove the protractor and use a ruler to join the vertex to your dot. This is the second arm.

Add a small curved arc between the two arms and label the angle 62° so anyone can read it.

The same care about scales applies. Always start counting from the 0° that lies on your first arm, not from the other end. If you want a 62° angle but you count from the wrong zero, you will accidentally draw 118° instead (because 180° − 62° = 118°). Estimating helps here too: 62° should look a little less than a square corner, so if your drawing looks obtuse you know to try again.
concepts.example: A good habit is to check your own drawing by measuring it. After you draw an angle you believe is 62°, measure it as if it were somebody else’s work. If it reads 62°, you can trust your method. Maryam draws each new angle twice and measures both; when they agree she knows her technique is solid. Neat labelling matters as well – a drawing with an unmarked angle is like a letter with no address, because no one can tell which angle you meant.

concepts.title: Angles on a Straight Line and Around a Point
concepts.explanation:
Now we move from measuring angles to calculating them using rules. The first two rules are about how angles fit together.

Angles on a straight line add to 180°. A straight line is a straight angle, a half turn, so any angles sitting along one side of a straight line must together make 180°. If one angle on a straight line is 130°, the angle next to it must be 180° − 130° = 50°. If three angles sit along a straight line and two of them are 60° and 70°, the third must be 180° − 60° − 70° = 50°.

Angles around a point add to 360°. All the way around a single point is a full turn, 360°. So if several angles meet at a point and share the whole turn between them, they must add to 360°. If three angles around a point are 150°, 120° and an unknown angle, the unknown is 360° − 150° − 120° = 90°. This is like sharing a whole circular anjero into slices: however you cut it, the slices together fill the full 360°.

Both rules work the same way: add up the angles you know, then subtract from the total (180° for a straight line, 360° around a point) to find the missing angle. Always ask yourself which total applies – is this a straight line, or a whole turn around a point? Looking carefully at the diagram tells you which rule to use.
concepts.example: You can check an answer by adding everything back up. If the angles on your straight line come to exactly 180°, and the angles around your point come to exactly 360°, your working is consistent. Omar always adds his angles back together as a final check – it catches slips before they become wrong answers.

methods.title: How to measure an angle with a protractor
methods.example: You measure an angle that looks sharp and clearly smaller than a square corner. The protractor arm crosses near both 40° and 140°. Which is correct?
steps: Estimate the angle first using a benchmark such as 45°, 90° or 180°.
Put the centre point of the protractor on the vertex.
Line up one arm along the baseline (the 0° line).
Read where the other arm crosses, choosing the scale that matches your estimate.

methods.title: How to draw an angle of a given size
methods.example: Draw an angle of 128° using a ruler and protractor, labelling the vertex, arms and angle clearly.
steps: Draw one arm with a ruler and mark the vertex at one end.
Put the protractor centre on the vertex, baseline along the arm.
Count from 0° to your angle and make a small dot.
Join the vertex to the dot, add an arc, and label the angle.

methods.title: How to find a missing angle
methods.example: Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 118°. Find the other.
steps: Decide which rule fits: straight line, point, triangle or quadrilateral.
Add up all the angles you already know.
Subtract that total from 180° or 360° (whichever the rule uses).
Check by adding your angles back to the correct total.

methods.title: Angles around a point
methods.example: Four angles meet at a point: 90°, 100°, 80° and an unknown angle x. Find x.
steps: Angles around a point add to 360°.
Add the known angles: 90° + 100° + 80° = 270°.

methods.title: Vertically opposite angles
methods.example: Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles is 65°. Find the other three.
steps: The angle vertically opposite the 65° is also 65°.
Each of the remaining two angles is on a straight line with 65°, so each is 180° − 65° = 115°, and they are vertically opposite each other so they match.
The four angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°.
Check: they add to 360°.

methods.title: Missing angle in a triangle
methods.example: A triangle has angles of 47° and 68°. Find the third angle.
steps: The angles add to 180°.

workedExamples.title: Classify an angle
workedExamples.solution: 155° is greater than 90° but less than 180°, so it falls in the obtuse range. It is an obtuse angle. (It is not reflex, because reflex angles must be more than 180°.)

workedExamples.title: Reading the correct scale
workedExamples.prompt: You measure an angle that looks sharp and clearly smaller than a square corner. The protractor arm crosses near both 40° and 140°. Which is correct?
workedExamples.solution: The angle looks acute, so it must be less than 90°. Of the two readings, only 40° is acute. The 140° reading came from the wrong scale. Estimating first told us immediately which number to trust.

workedExamples.title: Angles on a straight line
workedExamples.prompt: Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 118°. Find the other.
workedExamples.solution: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. So the other angle is 180° − 118° = 62°. Check: 118° + 62° = 180°. ✓

workedExamples.title: Angles around a point
workedExamples.prompt: Four angles meet at a point: 90°, 100°, 80° and an unknown angle x. Find x.
workedExamples.solution: Angles around a point add to 360°. Add the known angles: 90° + 100° + 80° = 270°. Then x = 360° − 270° = 90°. Check: 90° + 100° + 80° + 90° = 360°. ✓

workedExamples.title: Vertically opposite angles
workedExamples.prompt: Two straight lines cross. One of the four angles is 65°. Find the other three.
workedExamples.solution: The angle vertically opposite the 65° is also 65°. Each of the remaining two angles is on a straight line with 65°, so each is 180° − 65° = 115°, and they are vertically opposite each other so they match. The four angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°. Check: they add to 360°. ✓

workedExamples.title: Missing angle in a triangle
workedExamples.prompt: A triangle has angles of 47° and 68°. Find the third angle.
workedExamples.solution: The angles add to 180°. Third angle = 180° − 47° − 68° = 65°. Check: 47° + 68° + 65° = 180°. ✓

workedExamples.title: Isosceles triangle
workedExamples.prompt: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40°, and the two base angles are equal. Find the base angles.
workedExamples.solution: The two base angles share what is left after the vertex angle. Together they are 180° − 40° = 140°. Since they are equal, each is 140° ÷ 2 = 70°. Check: 40° + 70° + 70° = 180°. ✓

workedExamples.title: Missing angle in a quadrilateral
workedExamples.prompt: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 100°, 85° and 75°. Find the fourth.
workedExamples.solution: Angles in a quadrilateral add to 360°. Add the known angles: 100° + 85° + 75° = 260°. Fourth angle = 360° − 260° = 100°. Check: 100° + 85° + 75° + 100° = 360°. ✓

workedExamples.title: Two rules in one problem
workedExamples.prompt: In a right-angled triangle one of the non-right angles is 32°. A straight line is then extended from the 32° corner. Find (a) the third angle of the triangle and (b) the angle next to the 32° on the straight line.
workedExamples.solution: (a) The triangle has a 90° angle and a 32° angle, so the third is 180° − 90° − 32° = 58°. (b) The angle next to 32° on the straight line is 180° − 32° = 148°. Two different rules, each giving one certain answer.

activities.title: Angle Hunt Around the Home
activities.materials: a notebook, a pencil, and your sharp eyes.
steps: Walk through your home and find one example of each type of angle: acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex.
Sketch each one and label it with its type and your estimate of its size in degrees.
Look for right angles especially – doors, windows, tables, books. Why do you think builders use so many right angles?
Share your five best examples with your teacher at your next session.
Tip: the corner where a wall meets the floor is a right angle; a slightly open door makes an acute or obtuse angle depending on how far it swings.

activities.title: Make a Paper Protractor Angle Tester
steps: Fold the square exactly in half, then in half again, to make a folded corner. Open it out.
The single fold makes a straight line – that is 180°. The double fold makes a right angle – that is 90°.
Fold once more to make a 45° corner. You now have a simple tester for 45°, 90° and 180°.
Hold your folded tester against angles around the home and decide whether each angle is smaller than, equal to, or larger than a right angle.

activities.title: The Triangle Tear (180° Investigation)
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, a pencil and scissors.
steps: Draw any triangle you like and cut it out.
Tear off the three corners of the triangle.
Arrange the three torn corners tip to tip along the straight edge of your ruler.
Notice they fit exactly along a straight line, showing the three angles add to 180°. Try it with a completely different triangle – does it still work?
This is a real proof you can hold in your hands: the corners of any triangle always make a straight angle.

activities.title: Clock Angle Game
activities.materials: a clock with hands, or a picture of one you can draw.
steps: Set or draw the hands at 3:00. What type of angle do they make? Estimate its size.
Now try 6:00, 9:00 and 12:00. Which times give a right angle, a straight angle, and a full turn?
Remember each hour mark is 30° apart (because 360° ÷ 12 = 30°). Use this to work out the angle at 2:00 and at 5:00.
Challenge a family member to name a time that gives an obtuse angle, then check with your estimate.

activities.title: Design a Tiled Pattern (Angles Around a Point)
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, a protractor and colouring pencils.
steps: Mark a point in the middle of your page. This is where several angles will meet.
Using your protractor, draw lines out from the point so the angles around it add to exactly 360°.
Try making four equal angles (each 90°), then six equal angles (each 60°). Check they add to 360° each time.
Colour the sections to make a pattern like the tiles or windows in a masjid. Angles around a point always fill the full 360°.

activities.title: Family Direction Challenge (Turns and Angles)
activities.materials: your family or friends and some open space.
steps: Stand facing one direction. Call out turns: ‘Turn 90° clockwise!’ ‘Turn 180°!’
After each turn, everyone says which way they now face and how far they turned in total.
Play ‘get back home’: give a series of turns and see who can return to their starting direction.
Talk about how four quarter-turns (4 × 90°) make one full turn of 360°.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand angles best? Which type of angle was hardest to spot? What surprised you about the triangle tear? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Types of Angles
rules.text: Acute: less than 90 degrees. Right: exactly 90 degrees. Obtuse: between 90 and 180 degrees. Straight: exactly 180 degrees. Reflex: between 180 and 360 degrees. Full turn: exactly 360 degrees.

rules.title: Angle Sum Rules
rules.text: Angles on a straight line add to 180 degrees. Angles around a point add to 360 degrees. Angles in a triangle add to 180 degrees. Angles in a quadrilateral add to 360 degrees.

rules.title: Vertically Opposite Angles
rules.text: When two straight lines cross, the angles opposite each other are equal. Neighbouring angles at the crossing add to 180 degrees.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A quadrilateral has three equal angles and a fourth angle of 120°. Find the size of each equal angle.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The three equal angles share 360° − 120° = 240°, so each is 240° ÷ 3 = 80°.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Two straight lines cross so that one angle is three times its neighbour on the line. Find all four angles.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Neighbours on a line: x + 3x = 180°, 4x = 180°, x = 45°; so 45° and 135°, and by vertically opposite angles all four are 45°, 135°, 45°, 135°.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Angles on a Straight Line and Around a Point.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Now we move from measuring angles to calculating them using rules. The first two rules are about how angles fit together. Angles on a straight line add to 180°. A straight line is a straight angle, a half turn, so any angles sitting along one side of a straight line must together make 180°. If one angle on a straight line is 130°, the angle next to it must be 180° − 130° = 50°. If three angles sit along a straight line and two of them are 60° and 70°, the third must be 180° − 60° − 70° = 50°.
